# areaOfEffect

*points inside, near and beyond a region's border*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/areaOfEffect)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=areaOfEffect)
[![CRAN downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/areaOfEffect)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=areaOfEffect)
[![Monthly downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/areaOfEffect)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=areaOfEffect)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/gcol33/areaOfEffect/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/gcol33/areaOfEffect/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/gcol33/areaOfEffect/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/gcol33/areaOfEffect)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

areaOfEffect labels points by where they lie relative to a region, such as species records inside Austria, in a band around its border, or too far away to count.

Each point inside the region is labelled core, each point in a buffer zone around it is labelled halo, and points beyond the buffer are dropped. Projection, buffering and the point-in-polygon tests run through [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) in one call. The buffer width comes from the region itself: the default makes the halo area equal to the core area, so "near the boundary" means the same for Luxembourg and Brazil. You can then compare core and halo records, weight them, and decide whether the halo belongs in your analysis.

areaOfEffect supports:

- **Countries by name or your own polygons.** [`aoe()`](https://gillescolling.com/areaOfEffect/reference/aoe.html) takes a country name or ISO code (`"Austria"`, `"AT"`), several countries, an sf polygon, or nothing, in which case it detects the countries that contain the points.
- **Coastlines.** `mask = "land"` clips the halo to land, and `area = 1` then finds the buffer that makes the halo equal to the core on the land that remains.
- **Borders between regions.** `aoe_border()` classifies points by side and distance from a line, with zones of equal area on each side, for example along an international border.
- **A minimum number of points.** `aoe_expand()` grows the buffer of each region until it holds a minimum number of points, within caps on area and distance.
- **Balanced samples.** `aoe_sample()` draws a sample stratified by core and halo, or by side of a border, when one class dominates.

The default buffer scale, `sqrt(2) - 1`, is the solution of `(1 + s)^2 - 1 = 1`: the region scaled by `1 + s` has twice its area, so the halo has the area of the core. Without a mask this holds exactly; with a mask the buffer is found by a secant search on the clipped area. [Theory](https://gillescolling.com/areaOfEffect/articles/theory.html) derives the default and compares it with other choices.

## Installation

```r
install.packages("areaOfEffect")
```

The development version installs from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/areaOfEffect")
```

## Usage

1. Classify points against a region with `aoe()`.
2. Count core and halo points per region with `aoe_summary()`.
3. Keep the classes your analysis needs, or draw a balanced sample with `aoe_sample()`.

The input is an sf object of points, or a data frame whose coordinate columns are detected by their names or set with `coords`, such as `coords = c("lon", "lat")`. The region is a country name or ISO code, an sf polygon, or left out.

```{r aoe}
library(sf)
library(areaOfEffect)

observations <- data.frame(
  id  = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  lon = c(14.5, 15.2, 16.8, 20.0),
  lat = c(47.5, 48.1, 47.2, 48.5)
)
result <- aoe(observations, "Austria")
result
```

Points A and B lie in Austria and are core, point C lies in the buffer zone east of the border and is halo, and point D, in Slovakia beyond the buffer, is dropped. The result is an sf object, so it goes straight into sf and ggplot2 workflows.

<p align="center"><img src="man/figures/austria-aoe.svg" alt="Outline of Austria inside the dashed outline of its area of effect, the ring between them having the same area as Austria" width="500"></p>

```{r summary}
aoe_summary(result)
```

## Buffers on land

The default buffer extends into anything around the region, including the sea, where terrestrial records cannot occur. `mask = "land"` clips the halo to land, and `area = 1` solves for the buffer that makes the halo equal to the core after clipping:

```r
aoe(df, "Portugal", mask = "land", area = 1, largest_polygon = FALSE)
```

`largest_polygon = FALSE` keeps Portugal's islands, which the default drops in favour of the largest polygon.

<p align="center"><img src="man/figures/portugal-mask.svg" alt="Portugal and its Atlantic islands, the unmasked area of effect extending into the Atlantic as a dashed outline, and the area of effect clipped to land filled" width="500"></p>

## Buffer size

`scale` sets the halo size relative to the core. The halo:core area ratio is `(1 + scale)^2 - 1`:

| Scale | Halo:core area |
|-------|----------------|
| `sqrt(2) - 1` (default) | 1:1 |
| `0.5` | 1.25:1 |
| `1` | 3:1 |

[Theory](https://gillescolling.com/areaOfEffect/articles/theory.html#the-scale-parameter) explains when another scale suits an analysis.

## Documentation

Start with [Quick Start](https://gillescolling.com/areaOfEffect/articles/quickstart.html): points classified against a country, against your own polygons and several regions, and with a coastline mask.

- [Theory](https://gillescolling.com/areaOfEffect/articles/theory.html): why the default buffer has the area of the core, the buffer and stamp methods, and masks.
- [Full reference](https://gillescolling.com/areaOfEffect/reference/): every function, grouped by job.

## Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the [GitHub issues](https://github.com/gcol33/areaOfEffect/issues). A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with [reprex](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/).
